title: the flute
tomorrow: the rasa lila (with the Keeper's framing)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flute again: a gopi jealous of a piece of bamboo, until she looked at the rivers and trees that raised it and found herself glad. Did you find one thing to be glad about in someone else's good luck? Day eight hundred ninety-nine.
screen: `THE FLUTE.` · `JEALOUS OF A REED, THEN GLAD.`

segments.voice: The milk is on the fire. Someone is halfway through milking a cow. Someone is spooning food onto a plate for her family. Someone has a baby at her breast. It's an autumn night in Vraja, the moon is full and coming up red over the trees, and every house is in the middle of something. Then, from the forest, the flute. Not the daytime music the gopis talked about from a distance. This time, the Bhagavata says, the sound is calling them. Today, the flute, and what happens to everything they were holding.
screen: `THE MILK IS ON THE FIRE.` → `A FULL MOON OVER THE TREES.` → `THIS TIME, THE FLUTE CALLS.`

segments.voice: The text slows down here and goes house by house. The women hear the flute and they go, each one exactly as she is. The one milking leaves the cow. The one boiling milk leaves the pot on the fire. The one cooking leaves the food unserved. The one feeding a child, the one waiting on her husband, the one eating her own dinner, all of them stand up and leave it. Some were in the middle of dressing or putting on makeup, and they go with their clothes and ornaments still in disarray. Their husbands, fathers and brothers try to stop them, and they don't turn around. The Bhagavata adds that some were kept inside, unable to get out, and those women shut their eyes and went to him in meditation instead. Why linger on the half-finished jobs? Because the list is the point. Nobody in it has finished anything. Nobody waits for a better time, or tidies up, or makes herself presentable first. Devotional readers have heard in these lines a picture of the soul when God calls: it doesn't arrive polished, it arrives as it is, mid-task, with the milk still on the stove. And the Bhagavata doesn't let the scene pass unexamined. Right after this, the king who's listening stops the story to ask how a love like theirs could set anyone free, and Krishna himself will tell the women to go home. That is where we'll begin tomorrow. For tonight, the scene is enough. A village full of unfinished things, and a road into the trees with women on it, running toward a sound.
screen: `EACH ONE GOES EXACTLY AS SHE IS.` · `SOME KEPT INSIDE GO IN MEDITATION.` · `NOBODY FINISHES ANYTHING FIRST.` · then, large: `MID-TASK, AS SHE IS.`

segments.voice: Before you settle, notice what you've just set down to be here: a phone, a cup, a thought, a list. Don't tidy it. Leave it where it is. Now sit, and let your attention come here as you are, unfinished, not ready, no need to be. When the half-done things tug at you, notice the tug, and stay. If you pray, you can come to God, or to Krishna, just as you are in this moment, without fixing anything first. The bell holds the time.
The flute. On the autumn night, the sound that calls the gopis out of their houses, mid-task, just as they are.
Your line: the flute. Today, when someone you love calls for you, try answering once before you finish what you're doing. Day eight hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: The opening of the rasa lila chapters, with the gopis leaving their work at the sound of the flute, is recited and sung by Krishna devotees, and it is retold in dance and devotional poetry.

fork.setup: you're a gopi with milk boiling on the fire. on the full-moon night, the flute sounds from the forest, calling you. what do you do?
options: take the milk off the fire, then go.
leave the pot on the fire and go.
stay home and listen from the doorway.
fork.reveal: the Bhagavata says the one boiling milk left it on the fire: nobody finishes anything first. some kept inside went to him in meditation.

original.note: Sanskrit: autumn, the season of the full-moon night when the flute calls.

trapdoor: what you thought: the gopis go to hear some music.
what it means: each one leaves exactly what she was doing, mid-task, the moment the flute calls.
what a scholar hears: right after this, the Bhagavata has King Parikshit ask how a love like the gopis' could set them free, framing the scene before the dance.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.29, the autumn night: the flute calls and the gopis leave their tasks

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the list of interrupted tasks against Bhagavata 10.29 (roughly verses 4–8): milking, milk on the fire, cooking/serving, feeding children, serving husbands, eating, dressing and makeup; relatives trying to stop them; some kept inside who meditated on him.
The text says the women kept inside attained him in meditation (some readings: left their bodies); the script keeps only 'went to him in meditation'. A Keeper should decide how much to say.
'The moon coming up red' is in the scene-setting of 10.29.2 as I recall it; confirm or cut.
The line that the story 'isn't asking anyone to walk out on their family' anticipates the Keeper's framing for day 900; a Keeper may want to shape this.
The devotional reading (the soul arriving as it is) is attributed to 'devotional readers'; confirm.
Editor pass: review question now checks day 898's carry (turning envy into gladness) rather than the practice.

Audit: cut the narrator's own verdict ('the story isn't asking anyone to walk out on their family') and corrected Parikshit's question (10.29.12 asks how the gopis, knowing Krishna as a lover and not as Brahman, could be freed, not 'what kind of love this is'); the teach now points to his question and to Krishna sending the women home (10.29.18–27).
